First report of PLS(A) resistance gene sal(B) in multidrug-resistant foodborne Mammaliicoccus lentus: Molecular characterization and food safety implications
abstract: The emergence and dissemination of antimicrobial resistance through the food chain pose a significant threat to food safety and public health. Our nationwide surveillance of retail foods in China revealed alarmingly high resistance rates among foodborne Staphylococcus isolates, particularly to antibiotics targeting the 50S ribosomal subunit. Among these, Mammaliicoccus lentus (formerly Staphylococcus lentus) is a coagulase-negative species commonly found in food-producing animals and retail foods, increasingly recognized as a reservoir of antimicrobial resistance genes. To elucidate the genetic basis of this severe phenotype, we identified M. lentus strain M177 from retail potato flour exhibiting exceptionally high resistance to tiamulin, clindamycin, and lincomycin, a profile unexplained by known resistance genes. Targeted BLASTp analysis identified a putative ARE ABC-F gene sharing 98.71% amino acid identity with Sal(B), which we designated sal(B). Functional validation confirmed that Sal(B) confers specific resistance to PLS(pleuromutilins-lincosamides-streptogramin A) antibiotics, with tiamulin MIC increased by 128-fold, and clindamycin and lincomycin by 8-fold. Systematic alanine-scanning mutagenesis identified the Loop region as the primary effector of resistance, with Tyr251 playing a predominant role, while Ser262, Pro263, Gly266, Arg275, and Phe276 contributed to varying degrees. Structural analysis revealed an allosteric protection mechanism in which resistance-altering mutations disrupt specific interactions with 23S rRNA nucleotides within the peptidyl transferase center, rather than directly displacing antibiotics. ATP hydrolysis was strictly required for Sal(B) function. Genetic environment analysis indicated that sal(B) is chromosomal and likely intrinsic to M. lentus, with limited horizontal transfer potential. Notably, sal(B) or highly similar homologs were detected in geographically distinct food sources, suggesting a potential distribution that warrants further systematic surveillance. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of sal(B) in a foodborne M. lentus isolate, establishing Sal(B) as a mechanochemical allosteric regulator of PLSresistance. These findings highlight the need for enhanced surveillance of ARE ABC-F genes in foodborne coagulase-negative staphylococci beyond the traditional focus on S. aureus, due to the potential threat these resistance determinants pose to food safety and public health.

title: The next frontier in advanced practice nursing: Infectious diseases nurse practitioner certification
abstract: The increasing complexity of infectious diseases (ID) care, including antimicrobial stewardship, emerging pathogens, outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy, and expanding immunocompromised populations, has significantly broadened the role of nurse practitioners (NPs) in IDs practice. Concurrent challenges, including antimicrobial resistance, recurrent pandemics, evolving immunization guidelines, and vaccine hesitancy, further underscore the need for specialized expertise. This article proposes formal recognition of IDs as a NP subspecialty and outlines a framework for a postgraduate certification for Infectious Diseases Nurse Practitioners. The proposed competencies are grounded in the National Organization of Nurse Practitioner Faculties' NP Role Core Competencies and align with the 2021 American Association of Colleges of Nursing Essentials for Advanced Nursing Education. The framework also incorporates a One Health perspective, recognizing the interconnected influences of human, animal, and environmental health on ID management. Establishing a structured pathway for advanced training and certification may strengthen the NP workforce and enhance the delivery of comprehensive, evidence-based ID care.

A process-resolved risk prioritization framework reveals hidden antibiotic control deficiencies in wastewater treatment trains
abstract: Antibiotic prioritization in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) commonly relies on influent-effluent changes. Such assessments may mask differences among configurations, treatment contexts, and endpoint media. Here, we established a process-resolved antibiotic Environmental Health Prioritization index (PA-EHPi). At the configuration × antibiotic scale, PA-EHPi integrates effluent occurrence, apparent removal, ecological risk, and antimicrobial resistance selection pressure. Across anaerobic-anoxic-oxic (AAO), sequencing batch reactor (SBR), and membrane bioreactor (MBR) treatment configurations with broadly comparable influent antibiotic profiles and conventional pollutant removals, PA-EHPi revealed distinct priority profiles. PA-EHPi identified 2 of 22 antibiotics as priorities in AAO, 9 of 26 in SBR, and 9 of 24 in MBR. Azithromycin and clarithromycin remained priorities across all three configurations. Treatment-train diagnosis further revealed stable apparent removal in the sampled AAO plants, fluctuating removal in SBR plants, and significant terminal rebound in MBR plants. Linking PA-EHPi with sludge partitioning and antibiotic resistance gene profiles translated effluent priorities into endpoint-specific management pathways, identifying quinolones as dual effluent-sludge concerns, macrolides as effluent residual targets, tetracyclines as sludge-associated concerns, and chloramphenicols as resistance-background monitoring targets. Overall, the established PA-EHPi extends static effluent ranking into a process- and endpoint-resolved diagnostic framework, helping identify priority targets for antibiotic control and multimedia management in WWTPs.

title: Quantification of antimicrobial use in semi-intensive broiler farms in Kenya
abstract: The rapid global expansion of poultry production has intensified antimicrobial use (AMU) and emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Understanding patterns, timing, and quantities of AMU is essential for designing effective stewardship strategies. This study quantified AMU in semi-intensive broiler farms in Kenya using three complementary categories of metrics. Data were collected longitudinally from 73 farms across 310 production cycles over 10 months. Farmers recorded daily flock size and antibiotic administration using a standardized farm recording forms, and medicine packaging waste bins. AMU was quantified using complementary mass-based, dose-based, and count-based metrics. Overall, 16 antibiotics were administered in 68% production cycles, with 88% used in multi-antibiotic combinations. Use was predominant in early production stages, and treatment durations frequently deviated from the recommended 4-6 days; 81% of treated cycles were shorter or longer than recommended. A cumulative 292 mg/PCU was administered (mean 13 mg/PCU per cycle), with sulfadimidine, fosfomycin, and sulfamerazine accounting for the highest quantities. While 63% of antibiotics had mean UDD/DDD ratios within acceptable dosing range (0.8-1.2), treatment-course level analysis showed widespread dosing deviations, with both under- and overdosing. These findings demonstrate that a single AMU indicator can mask important exposure patterns. Integrating multiple metrics into surveillance systems is essential to guide targeted, context-specific antimicrobial stewardship in rapidly expanding poultry systems.
